ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure shows a unity negative feedback control system. The input R(s) enters the summing point from the left and is added at the positive terminal of the summing point; the output Y(s) is led out from the right, and at the same time returns to the negative terminal of the summing point through the lower feedback path. The output of the summing point is labeled E(s), and it enters the forward-path block G(s), whose output is Y(s). Reasoning: From the figure, one can write Y(s)=G(s)E(s), and since it is unity negative feedback, E(s)=R(s)-Y(s). Therefore E(s)=R(s)-G(s)E(s), namely E(s)=R(s)/(1+G(s)). Given G(s)=6/[s(s+1)(s+2)], the unit step input r(t) corresponds to R(s)=1/s, so E(s)=(1/s)/(1+6/[s(s+1)(s+2)])=(s+1)(s+2)/[s(s+1)(s+2)+6]. The denominator is s(s+1)(s+2)+6=s^3+3s^2+2s+6=(s+3)(s^2+2). Therefore the poles of E(s) are s=-3 and s=±j√2. s=-3 corresponds to a decaying exponential term, but s=±j√2 corresponds to an undamped sinusoidal oscillation term, so e(t) will continue to oscillate and will not converge to a finite limit.

If the input \( r(t) \) is a unit step function, what happens to \( e(t) \) as \( t \to \infty \)?
ready3_open_rewrite.resolved_answer: \( \lim_{t \to \infty} e(t) \) does not exist, \( e(t) \) is oscillatory
ready3_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure shows a unity negative feedback control system. The input R(s) enters the summing point from the left and is added at the positive terminal of the summing point; the output Y(s) is led out from the right, and at the same time returns to the negative terminal of the summing point through the lower feedback path. The output of the summing point is labeled E(s), and it enters the forward-path block G(s), whose output is Y(s). Reasoning: From the figure, one can write Y(s)=G(s)E(s), and since it is unity negative feedback, E(s)=R(s)-Y(s). Therefore E(s)=R(s)-G(s)E(s), namely E(s)=R(s)/(1+G(s)). Given G(s)=6/[s(s+1)(s+2)], the unit step input r(t) corresponds to R(s)=1/s, so E(s)=(1/s)/(1+6/[s(s+1)(s+2)])=(s+1)(s+2)/[s(s+1)(s+2)+6]. The denominator is s(s+1)(s+2)+6=s^3+3s^2+2s+6=(s+3)(s^2+2). Therefore the poles of E(s) are s=-3 and s=±j√2. s=-3 corresponds to a decaying exponential term, but s=±j√2 corresponds to an undamped sinusoidal oscillation term, so e(t) will continue to oscillate and will not converge to a finite limit.
